To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rise of the NUM was a compromise between the class forces of capital and labour on the mines; the compromise involved a significant degree of class power on the part of capital; and this power was exercised in part through a complex set of relations of power, which were not reducible to a single source of domination.

class compromise, understood as a process of negotiation between classes that results in a temporary balance of power in favour of a dominant group, is an appropriate way to understand the rise of the NUM on the South African mines.

the NUM, as a class organization, was able to achieve a class compromise with the mine management, which allowed for a substantial increase in wages for the miners, and which also allowed the NUM to gain control of the mines' welfare and recreational facilities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the rise to power of the NUM, and the exercise of that power in a particular historical and geographical context.

the following question: How can we understand class power on the South African mines, and the rise of the NUM in the context of a history of class struggle on the mines, using Erik Olin Wright’s explication of class compromises and Foucault’s notion of power as a relational force, rather than as a possession or attribute?
the following question: how did the NUM, a union that was formed in 1982 by the merger of two white and three black unions, come to dominate the gold mines by 1985?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
class compromise on the South African mines was, in the final analysis, a class struggle in which the working class was defeated.
the NUM was a class compromise, in which the class power of the mine-owners and the mine-workers was both modified and modified.

the NUM was not the product of class compromise, but of the exercise of power, and that this exercise of power was a complex, contradictory, and contingent process, in which the NUM, as a class organisation, was both the subject of power and the agent of power.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NUM, as a class organisation, has been successful, but only in the sense of a partial compromise.
the NUM's success was not the product of a single, decisive compromise, but rather a complex process of class compromise and class struggle that took place over the period of the 1980s.

the NUM's success on the gold mines was due to its ability to forge class compromises, but that the nature of the compromises, the parties to them, and their consequences, were far more complex than the simple model proposed by Wright.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the NUM's rise and consolidation of power in the 1980s and early 1990s was not a straightforward process, but was rather a series of compromises, some of them with the state, some with capital, some with other unions.
class compromise, while a useful heuristic, does not provide an adequate explanation of the rise and fall of the NUM on the South African mines.
the concept of power needs to be understood in terms of the relationship between the powerful and the powerless.
